records.description: Voted for Newton County's 2026 budget and the 2025 property tax rate on September 23, 2025. No member voted against. The adopted rate of $0.696645 per $100 of value was lower than the prior year's rate, and the county collected $2,861 less in property tax than the year before.

Represented father Keith Renfro in his appeal of a Rusk County ruling that ended his parental rights. The Sixth Court of Appeals in Texarkana affirmed the ruling on May 26, 2005, so his client lost the appeal.

Granted a new trial on November 21, 2018 in a divorce the parties had already settled in mediation, one day after the husband filed the request on his own. The Twelfth Court of Appeals in Tyler ruled on January 9, 2019 that he abused his discretion and directed him to cancel the order.

Published a law review comment on June 5, 2018 arguing that Texas law makes it too hard for third-party parents, such as stepparents and other caregivers, to bring a custody suit. She wrote that the strict standing rules keep courts from reaching the best interest of the child. It ran in the Texas A&M Law Review, volume 5, pages 563 to 593.

Served as the court-appointed lawyer for two children (attorney ad litem) in an appeal over ending a parent's rights, from Lamar County Court at Law. The Sixth Court of Appeals in Texarkana upheld the trial court on January 18, 2022, case 06-21-00100-CV.

Served as the court-appointed lawyer for five children (attorney ad litem) in an appeal over ending a parent's rights, from the 62nd District Court in Lamar County. The Sixth Court of Appeals in Texarkana upheld the trial court on November 3, 2023, case 06-23-00057-CV.

Sentenced Timothy Mitchell to 200 days in jail for attacking two people on Austin's Congress Avenue bridge, and approved the plea deal prosecutors asked for. She said she felt compelled to approve it, and that state law let her order mental health treatment only if the defendant got probation, which he could not because he had no home address.

Made the motion on December 3, 2024 to let the county judge sign the forms joining the county to opioid settlements offered by the Kroger Co. The county is a plaintiff in Panola County v. Purdue Pharma. The court approved it unanimously.

Made the motion on October 21, 2025 to turn down CenterPoint Energy's request to lay a 4-inch high pressure gas line along Panola County Roads 232, 202 and 201. Residents and utility representatives spoke first. The court voted it down unanimously.
Issued a disaster declaration for Cass County on January 25, 2026 after Winter Storm Fern, and closed county offices the following day.
Moved to start the 30-day notice needed to cancel the county tax break for the Cattlemen I solar project, run by EDP Solar, on July 22, 2024. The motion passed with no votes against.
Ordered Balmorhea Lake and Red Bluff Lake closed for Easter weekend as part of Reeves County's COVID-19 disaster orders. The closure order expired on April 12, 2020.
Signed Reeves County Order No. 5 as county judge. The order declared a local disaster over the COVID-19 outbreak and required businesses in the county to make people wear face coverings.

Asked the Gillespie County Commissioners Court on October 10, 2022 to set pay for election workers, the first year the county put them on its payroll. She proposed $10.25 an hour for new election clerks, $11.25 for experienced clerks, and $11.50 for election judges. The court approved her rates and added a 5 percent raise for bilingual clerks and judges.

Raised a concern about a plan to pay Fort Stockton farmers to pump less groundwater, in an article published July 22, 2021. Ramos said farmers could be pulled away from a crop with a proven record of selling well. He backed the other half of the plan, better irrigation equipment, saying he was fully on board with the efficiency work.

Testified against Texas Senate Bill 261 at a state Senate committee hearing on March 31, 2025. The bill banned the sale of lab-grown meat in Texas for two years. The official witness list names her as a founder from Austin speaking for herself.

Publicly opposed the Texas ban on selling lab-grown meat in a Texas Standard story published September 9, 2025. The ban took effect September 1, 2025. She said she kept working on her lab-grown brisket anyway.

Cast the only vote against dropping the county's employee salary survey at a special Karnes County Commissioners Court meeting on August 7, 2019. She had asked the court to hold a workshop on the survey before setting the budget. The county judge moved to take no action on the survey and that motion passed 3-1.

Backed a 90-day extension of federal COVID-19 paid leave for Karnes County employees, reported on March 26, 2021. She and Commissioner James Rosales proposed the 90-day term, and she was the only commissioner to vote for it. The court then passed a 30-day extension instead by a 4-1 vote.

Seconded the motion that adopted Lee County's official position on the Sandow Lakes Energy natural gas power plant. The resolution welcomed the plant but asked the company to look at other sites on the same ranch, farther from homes in the Blue and Adina area. The court adopted it with no votes against, and Commissioner Richard Wagner was absent. At the same meeting Knobloch said the governor, the state senator, and the state representative had all spoken in favor of the plant.
Moved to hire Rawley McCoy & Associates as the architect for a new county office and shop in Precinct 4, on October 23, 2023, and to let the county judge start contract talks. The court agreed 5-0.

Moved to put DeWitt County into a five-year equipment lease with Motorola Solutions on October 27, 2025, under a state purchasing contract. The lease can be canceled if the county does not fund it in a later year. The court approved it 5-0.

Signed a tax abatement agreement with ZSS Power LLC on February 10, 2025 as Knox County Commissioner, Precinct 2. The agreement cancels 100 percent of Knox County property taxes on the company's solar project for ten years. It replaced an earlier 2022 deal and added land the company had bought.

Signed a tax abatement agreement with Wagon Timber Solar LLC on March 10, 2025 as Knox County Commissioner, Precinct 2. The agreement cancels 100 percent of Knox County property taxes on the company's solar and battery project for ten years. The company must be running the plant by December 31, 2028 to keep the tax break.

Signed a county resolution on May 12, 2025 creating the Wagon Timber Solar Reinvestment Zone #2. The zone marks the land where Knox County can give a solar company a property tax break, and it runs for five years.

Signed a tax abatement agreement with Rolling Plains Solar LLC on November 10, 2025 as Knox County Commissioner, Precinct 2. The agreement cancels 100 percent of Knox County property taxes on the company's solar project for ten years.
Moved to open talks on a property tax break for a wind repower project in Coke County on May 27, 2025, after a presentation by Gerald Byrd of Ernst and Young. The motion carried.

Moved to adopt a property tax break deal with Goat Wind, L.L.C. and to let the county judge sign it, on January 12, 2026. The motion carried. At the same meeting he moved to pass a resolution backing a state law to exempt Texas counties from the state hotel tax, which also carried.
Moved to accept a sealed bid of $135,808 from Harrison Roofing for a new roof on the Coke County courthouse on February 23, 2026. The motion carried.

Served as the lawyer for two Dallas-area businessmen who sued the Texas attorney general in federal court over their child-support collection business. The court entered judgment for the attorney general on September 30, 2005, and the plaintiffs lost.

Spoke to the Burnet County Commissioners Court as a board member of Opportunities for Burnet and Williamson Counties in favor of a property tax exemption for the nonprofit. The court adopted a 50 percent exemption for 2025.

Moved to add a sixth Election Day voting site in Briggs on August 24, 2021, saying the trip to vote ran 73 to 75 miles round trip and the extra site cost about $800 to $1,000. No other commissioner seconded it, so it died. He then cast the only vote against the five-site plan the court adopted 4-1.

Moved to add a deputy county clerk job to the 2022-2023 county budget, paid from unspent funds. The motion failed 2-3. He then cast the only vote against the $31 million budget the court adopted 4-1 on August 23, 2022.
Voted against a county letter of support for Lonestar Faith LLC to work as a new ambulance provider in Burnet County. The request failed 2-3 on May 12, 2026.

Waited more than 10 hours at the Texas Capitol on July 29, 2026 to testify against the 765-kilovolt power line before the Texas Senate Committee on Business and Commerce. He told the committee most of his constituents saw the project as a trampling of their property rights.
Sentenced a 39-year-old man to 75 years in prison on May 4, 2026 after a Calhoun County jury found him guilty of continuous sexual abuse of a child under 14.

Jailed a Bee County father for contempt of court after he failed to pay child support and medical support. The order set 180 days in jail and found he owed about $15,090 in child support and $12,353 in medical support. The Thirteenth Court of Appeals refused to free him on December 22, 2014 and let her order stand.

Filed a proposed Lamar County general revenue budget of $12,196,718 for 2023-24. The plan rested on a tax rate of 30.45 cents per $100 of property value, the highest rate allowed without a public vote and almost 4 cents below the 2022 rate.
Brought forward six settlement participation and release forms in the Texas opioid lawsuit. The commissioners court approved them and authorized him to sign the documents for the county.
Seconded a motion to bar alcohol from the Limestone County Fairgrounds Annex building, then moved to bar fireworks from the fairgrounds parking lot. Both passed 3-1, and he voted yes on each.

Moved to hire Outdoor Management Services to spray herbicide along Limestone County road ditches for weed and brush control. Residents had spoken against the spraying at earlier meetings. The motion failed 2-3, with Anderson and Commissioner Jody Goodman voting yes.

Moved to hire the law firm Linebarger Goggan Blair and Sampson to collect the county's unpaid accounts, and to add an extra penalty to those bills to cover the collection cost. The motion passed 3-0, with Commissioner Stephen Friday abstaining.

Moved to accept election grant money on September 28, 2020, including $19,952 from the Center for Tech and Civic Life for the Hopkins County Clerk's office. The clerk said the money paid for voter information and protective equipment at polling places. The court approved it unanimously.

Made two motions on December 12, 2022 that helped the Pine Forest Solar project. One approved the first amendment to the county's agreement with Pine Forest Solar I LLC and Pine Forest Hybrid I LLC. The other approved an expanded reinvestment zone for Pine Forest Solar I LLC, which sets the area eligible for tax breaks. Both passed unanimously.

Moved to approve a resolution opposing the end of the countywide polling place program on March 25, 2025. That program lets a Hopkins County voter cast a ballot at any polling place in the county instead of only at their own precinct. The court approved the resolution unanimously.
